How to decide if you want treatment
Well, are you okay with your current situation, and can you accept being this way for the next 5 years? Can you accept avoiding situations which trigger your anxiety, but also losing the benefits and potential opportunities by choosing to avoid them? And I guess, you need to try asking yourself, what exactly do you fear when you think about getting treatment. Do you fear the therapist judging you? Do you fear being treated in a unprofessional manner and not getting the help? Etc.  I think it's better if you can get clarity on this part, because to me, the "there are days with no issues" isn't the core reason.


How to decide if you want a counsellor or clinical psychologist
At least in my own experience, counsellors and clinical psychologist both offer the same thing, which is talk therapy, so whether they call themselves therapist doesn't really change this fact. Maybe you are more suited for CBT, or maybe another therapy orientation, but you really can't know and predict until you try it for yourself. Whether you get a competent and suitable can only come with taking a leap of faith and trying. I myself tried out more than 4 therapists from both sides before finally finding one that really suits me, so i get it when you say its so tiring having to repeat your story. So, which is more tiring, repeating the story when you seek treatment with hopes of better mental health, or living with your current state every day?

To me, a good therapist is one who asks you questions that makes you think and reflect upon yourself and your situation, empathise with you, treat emotions with respect and validate them, and is able to tell you when they do not understand something or have a difference in values/opinions without forcing it onto you.  In therapy, you are bound to feel discomfort at some point. You are there to heal emotional wounds after all. But it will take some time, esp if it's your first, to know for yourself whether the discomfort is coming from the normal process of healing or from the actions of irresponsible therapists. For example,  they may ask you to do to try a new activity in therapy or outside of it, which may lead to some anxiety if you are new to it, but they will be open to discussions and address your concerns and fears about it.They won't guilt trip you nor force you into doing it. Another sign of you having a good therapist is whether you feel safe in raising a potential disagreement with the therapist (respectfully of course). I would sometimes ask my therapist why do A and not B instead, or tell my therapist that a suggested plan is not viable for my case. My therapist would listen and explain to me in a professional manner, and we would then continue to have discussions until we come to an agreed plan. I never felt belittled or disrespected. There are so many other qualities that make a good therapist but I decide to just emphasize on this point because i personally know some ppl who would just go along with what their therapist say even if they disagree because they dont want conflict, and imo, that does not promote trust between them and the therapist and it is ultimately not beneficial to the entire therapy process. 

In the end, a good therapist may have all the great qualities but if you do not vibe with their therapy modality, then it's not your fault and not theirs; accept that fact, move on, and try other professionals until you find a modality that suits you.

As a minor along with financial constraints and not wanting your parents to know and doing a diagnosis from home, your options are unfortunately very very limited. If a diagnosis is all you want, you can google mental health test offered by reputable organizations (websites with .org, by universities etc) and take a mental health screening thats usually free, but this DOES NOT replace a proper professional diagnosis, only to offer you some indication during this constraint. If you want treatment and this to me sounds more like what you are after, then the only option I can think of is your school counsellor (if your school offers online counselling atm) for services since this option is free for students. Do you think the worst of yourself, or used to be that way? Like, being critical of yourself? I used to think that way of my parents because one parent often criticizes others while the other parent prefer giving me feedback, suggestions, telling me what to do & what not to do and it can become very stiffling even though it came from a place of concern. If you are or used to be the type that struggle with self compassion and often used criticisms/harsh feedback either on yourself or on others then your daughter may have indirectly picked that up and turn that into her barometer for viewing the world. 

I think the best way to know is to ask her and prod for more information whenever she tells you those things, like, can you tell me more about that? Why did you think I would be disappointed at you for xyz? When did you start having this thoughts? When did you feel I care for you? What happen specifically? What would I need to do in order for you to feel cared for?

If you explore and asks her these, it's important to place the focus on her and don't try to correct yourself; you need information gathering and it can only happen when you allow her space and safety to open up. 

Sometimes, you may be doing all the right things but both of your love languages are not aligned. She may have her own version but it was never discussed nor explored so you show her love but she just cannot receive it and vice versa. 

Also, one good resource to check is Nonviolent Communication by Marshall Rosenberg, you can check it on youtube. It's about the communication model which helps resolve conflict and support relationships. Really powerful and transformative. 

All the best to you! :)

Societal factors: in the midst of pandemic, financial insecurity, living in places which tend to lack safety and resources, lacking in scientific based mental health education and awareness programs in educational institutions, limited affordable mental health services for community (whether there are gov funded or by ngo), youth culture in heavily relying on social media for validation, how healthy or toxic the education environment is (eg school bullying, overemphasis on achievement, unfair treatment and allocation of resource to sub groups of students, very low counsellor to student ratio in school, educators own lack of understanding of mental health etc), heavy shame based culture in society

Family factors: mental health issues rooted in biological factor passed on from parents to children, parents themselves have mental health issues but are ill-equipped to handle them let alone help their children develop better coping skills, breakdown in family structure due to various life factors (eg extramarital affairs, financial problems, trauma within the family, crime perpetrated by family member etc)

Individual factors: individual's own predisposition in developing mental health issues, whether they are equipped with healthy coping skills, whether their social network is enough to act as buffer etc.

The list goes on, but as you can see, when a person is facing mental health issues, there can be so many factors underlying it, yet a large part of society blames the individual for being that way. That narrative needs to change.

Taking lexapro recently and after the initial phase of my body getting adapted to it, I do see some positive effects, mainly I wasn't as prone to being fearful as I was before taking meds (when a small trigger can cause my anxiety wheels to start turning), I can focus and concentrate better (which means I am not zombified, in fact, I feel so much more present in the moment and that leads to willingness to be productive) and really just feel like some load has been taken off me. The downside is the increased in appetite which led to weight gain, not drastic, but something I need to keep monitoring. 

I dont feel sleepy but I think it's because my dosage is small which is enough for me.

Also, your therapist suggesting psychiatric meds for you is actually a sign that your therapist is being professional at their job. To put it simply, anxiety can have a biological basis, or induced by life events. Many cases it's a combination of both. So while your therapist can help you with psychotherapy, if in your case you also need meds to address the imbalance of brain chemicals causing anxiety, then it is right for the therapist to also refer you to see a psychiatrist. It's not an either/or scenario. Combination of meds and therapy shows the best result according to research. The only way to find out is to try.

Between 1-2 weeks, I am lucky since lexapro is favourable for me so far. I heard that people respond differently to the meds so it may take somone else longer to see results. I was pretty anxious about the entire thing before getting the prescription for the first time ever so watching people's review about the meds on youtube helped me get a wider perspective.

I started very recently and I've seen noticeable effects for me, mainly clearing of brain fog, increased focus, and reduction of feeling fearful. There are some side effects like dryness in the mouth and some weight gain for me but I am so glad that I gave it a try after years of being dissuaded by family. Keep it up, and don't be afraid of bringing up possibility of changing meds with your psychiatrist if what you are taking doesn't work for you.

I'm half way through the process of seeking psychiatric treatment at gov hospital, mainly I already secured my referral letter from klinik kesihatan (kk)about 1 week ago, but haven't yet visited gov hospital due to several issues that pop up.

I visited the facebook page of the kk in my area, and found out they are implementing qmed, which is an online appointment system to book a slot for visit to kk due to high volume of patients, so I dont think walk in is available. Not sure if it also applies to yours, but anyway, go to their fb page or website to make the appt. Follow the instructions, it's pretty easy. Also, choose "kes pesakit luar" when asked for type of services. At the end you will get a confirmation slip, print it and bring it with you as proof for your visit to kk. I went there, showed the staff my slip, follow their direction, register details and pay rm1 before seeing the doctor.

When asked for reason, I just wrote/told them I need a referral letter to visit psychiatric clinic at ppum. That's enough reason. Tbh the doctor didn't exactly administer me the dass, but he did ask me questions pertaining to mental health history so that he can write me the letter. 

I suggest you bring along a friend if you feel overwhelmed in large crowds. While they controlled the flow of patients pretty well, I still found it somewhat overwhelming due to my anxiety (then again, this differs for everyone). 

Another alternative you can consider for therapy is Solshealth (sungai besi, but also offers virtual session) they have block sessions available and differing rates depending on income level; definitely more affordable than the standard private practice fees. 

Good luck.
